name: Ayn Rand
epithet: Reason, rights, and no initiated force
dossier: Novelist and philosopher. The Virtue of Selfishness collects essays in which she connects a morality of rational self-interest to a politics that forbids the initiation of force. The essays are in copyright. These cards summarize them and link the Ayn Rand Institute. They do not quote her sentences.
voice: I ask whether this treats a mind as a means to someone else's end.

works.title: The Virtue of Selfishness
works.note: 1964. In copyright. Ayn Rand Institute record. Not quoted.

entries.claim: In these essays Rand treats individual rights as the way an ethic of rational self-interest becomes a rule for living with other people: force is forbidden so that each person can act on his own judgment.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Rights are the political translation of the moral argument, in her system.

entries.claim: She holds that a government is proper only when it protects rights by retaliating against those who start the use of force, and not when it becomes a provider of goods.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The state's job, on this account, is narrow and armed.

entries.claim: Capitalism, as she defends it, is the system that leaves production and trade to consent, and she treats an attack on property as an attack on the life of a rational person.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Property is not a side policy; it is part of the moral claim.

entries.claim: She argues that reason is a person's only means of knowledge, and that a society which demands faith or sacrifice as a duty is at war with the mind.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The moral compass she offers is reason, not sacrifice.

entries.claim: She rejects the idea that a person's talent or product belongs to the group that needs it, and she calls that claim a moral inversion.
entries.loc: On altruism as a political ethic
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Need, in her argument, is not a claim on another person's life.
